summary: Discovery focused on unit economics across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Galileo described latency and budget constraints for a customer-facing chat product and internal analytics tooling. We discussed per-token math, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, quantization tradeoffs, and a proposed micro-benchmark. Security and procurement questions (SOC2, SSO, KMS) were raised. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing workbook and run benchmark; Galileo to share prompt set and traffic profile.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Lina Rodriguez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Lina from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. We also have Marcus Chen, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Sharma: Hey Lina, thanks. Good here, appreciate you making time.
[00:11] Daniel Ortiz: Hi all, Daniel here. I left the calendar with a little buffer but yeah, excited to unpack costs.
[00:18] Aisha Khan: Aisha from procurement, I'll mostly be listening but will ask on SKUs and contract bits.
[00:24] Marcus Chen: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: understand Galileo's workload shape, budget constraints, latency targets, then walk through per-token math and levers like batching, caching, quantization, and deployment modes.
[00:33] Priya Sharma: Perfect. To set context, we have two primary workloads: 1) a customer-facing chat assistant for financial advisors — high concurrency, low-ish tokens per request (avg 350 tokens), strict p95 latency target under 250ms; 2) internal analytics summarization jobs — larger sequences, up to 4k tokens, can be async.
[00:52] Daniel Ortiz: Our immediate ask is to see if we can pilot with Hosted first but our procurement prefers a path to Dedicated or Private in case of data residency and contract terms. Budget for first 6 months is capped at about $85k.
[01:10] Lina Rodriguez: Thanks, that's super helpful. On the price side, we typically present two flavors: Hosted (Redwood API) with usage-based billing and Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput. Private is available for customers who need VPC/on-prem and a different license structure.
[01:27] Marcus Chen: To ground the discussion, can you confirm expected QPS during peak and average sequence length distribution?
[01:34] Priya Sharma: Peak concurrent users maybe 1200 sessions, QPS ~150-200, avg sequence per message ~350 as I said, and we have bursts up to 400 QPS for short periods.
[01:44] Marcus Chen: OK so with 200 QPS and ~350 tokens per turn, rough token rate's 70k tokens/sec. But important distinction: when we say tokens, are you counting user prompt plus model output?
[01:56] Priya Sharma: Yes, it's total tokens including system prompt, user message and generated tokens. Typically generation is around 90 tokens per response.
[02:04] Marcus Chen: Noted. Aisha, from procurement side, what are your contract constraints?
[02:09] Aisha Khan: Mainly we need clear unit pricing, a cap option or alerts before spend thresholds, and SOC2-type attestation. Also KMS integration is a big checkbox.
[02:18] Lina Rodriguez: Completely understood. On SOC2 and KMS we can share our compliance pack and docs; we support customer-managed keys with Redwood Private and dedicated KMS integrations for Dedicated as well.
[02:28] Daniel Ortiz: Quick practical question — you mentioned caching: how much lift does prefix or KV cache give for a chat use case?
[02:35] Marcus Chen: It varies. If you have a lot of repeated system prompts or template responses, prefix caching can reduce generation tokens. KV cache (we sometimes say "K V cash" in transcripts, sorry) reduces compute when users navigate back to similar contexts because we can reuse KV cache across sequences. For pure chat where prompts differ, you'll still benefit from request-level caching for exact-match prompts or embedding-based retrieval caches. Realistically, for a moderately templated chat you might see 10-35% token reduction from caching strategies.
[03:03] Priya Sharma: That's helpful. On quantization — we've been thinking of 4-bit or 8-bit models. How does that affect price?
[03:10] Marcus Chen: Quantization impacts the GPU memory footprint and therefore whether you can pack more replicas per GPU. In Dedicated/Private you can choose optimized quantized runtimes — cost per token can drop materially if you can run a smaller model or quantized variant. In Hosted we offer quantized-inference-backed model variants too; typically unit compute cost could reduce 20-50% depending on model and toolchain. But there's a quality tradeoff you need to validate with evals.
[03:34] Priya Sharma: Can you give a ballpark per-token math for the chat scenario?
[03:38] Lina Rodriguez: Sure. For illustration only: Hosted with our mid-sized open model might run about $0.8 to $1.5 per 1k generation tokens including infra + margin — sorry, these are example numbers, actual depends on model. If you enable batching and caching and use a quantized variant, unit cost can drop to sub-$0.5 per 1k tokens. Dedicated reserved capacity changes the math: you pay a monthly committed seat for GPU pool and then deliver much lower marginal per-token cost for high QPS workloads.
[04:06] Daniel Ortiz: Those hosted numbers seem high for our budget; with 70k tokens/sec peak that's massive if sustained.
[04:12] Marcus Chen: Right, sustained high throughput almost always pushes toward Dedicated or hybrid routing. Another lever is shaping traffic — e.g., use streaming vs full generation, reduce max_tokens, or add post-processing to avoid unnecessary tokens. Also can route less-sensitive traffic to lower-cost model variants.
[04:30] Priya Sharma: I want to understand the Dedicated break-even. At what sustained throughput does Dedicated make sense?
[04:35] Marcus Chen: Rough rule of thumb: if your sustained monthly token volume crosses into the multi-billion token range, Dedicated becomes cost-advantageous. But the exact math depends on your model choice, sequence lengths, and utilization. We'll run a break-even calc for you in the pricing workbook.
[04:50] Priya Sharma: Sounds good. Aisha: what would procurement need to see to approve a Dedicated pilot?
[04:55] Aisha Khan: Clear SLA language, data handling terms, proof of KMS and SSO integrations, and a defined burn-rate forecast for the pilot with cap/escape clauses.
[05:06] Lina Rodriguez: We can draft a pilot agreement template that includes monthly committed capacity, a spend cap, and an exit clause. We'll attach SOC2 and KMS docs.
[05:15] Daniel Ortiz: One technical curiosity: how does Redwood do automatic batching? If we have lots of short requests, can the runtime batch to increase utilization without violating p95 SLO?
[05:23] Marcus Chen: Our serving runtime has continuous batching with latency-aware policies. You set a per-route SLO, max acceptable latency and a batching window. The runtime will batch until either the batch fills or latency threshold is approached. For chat with strict 250ms p95, we favor smaller batches with lower latency targets — you still see some batching benefits but less than async jobs. If you can tolerate 20-40ms extra tail, batching can increase throughput substantially.
[05:50] Priya Sharma: Important to note: our p95 includes network time to our app plus inference. So we need to budget for 100-150ms round-trip for app, leaving 100ms for model inference ideally.
[06:01] Marcus Chen: Thanks, that clarifies. We'll craft the benchmark to measure p95 in our environment with similar network RTT and include warm/cold-start scenarios.
[06:09] Aisha Khan: On the security side again, for Private deployments, do you push the control plane into our VPC or is it an on-prem package?
[06:15] Lina Rodriguez: We offer both: a private control plane that talks to your VPC and an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. For the private control plane we integrate with your KMS and SSO. For on-prem it's a licensed install with additional support costs.
[06:28] Daniel Ortiz: Marcus, could the KV cache be shared across replicas if we go Dedicated?
[06:33] Marcus Chen: Yes, there are modes. We have shared cache layers and per-replica caches; sharing increases hit rate but needs coordination. For high concurrency live chat, a distributed cache often yields better overall hit rates. However, consistency and eviction policies need tuning relative to your prompt patterns.
[06:50] Priya Sharma: We're also very concerned about inference regressions. How do you handle regression monitoring if we roll models or quantized variants?
[06:57] Marcus Chen: Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and evals. You can pin a model version and set regression alerts on metrics like fidelity, hallucination rate, or token-level differences. For pilots we typically recommend baseline evals on a canonical prompt set and continuous sampling for production.
[07:14] Priya Sharma: Good, we'll want that in writing.
[07:17] Lina Rodriguez: We'll include the Optimize docs and sample alert rules.
[07:21] Daniel Ortiz: Any gotchas on embedding costs? We plan to do retrieval-augmented generation; embeddings could be a separate cost line.
[07:27] Marcus Chen: Yes, embeddings are billed separately typically and are cheaper per unit than generation but you must consider vector store costs and refresh frequency. If you do frequent re-embeddings, that can add up. We can model that in the workbook.
[07:38] Priya Sharma: Back to numbers — can we run a quick scenario? Suppose 200 QPS sustained with 445 tokens total per interaction (prompt+response) and 30% caching hit. What's a rough monthly spend on Hosted?
[07:50] Lina Rodriguez: Off the cuff, 200 QPS * 445 tokens = 89k tokens/sec, *3600*24 ~ 7.7B tokens/day, that's enormous. With 30% cache hit reduces to 5.4B/day. Multiply by 30 days ~162B tokens/month. At $1 per 1k tokens that's $162k/month — clearly beyond your 85k 6-month budget unless you route or throttle. This demonstrates why we need realistic QPS tails and to consider Dedicated.
[08:20] Daniel Ortiz: That's a useful wake-up call — our numbers were optimistic. We likely need to design for lower sustained QPS and rely on burst capacity.
[08:28] Marcus Chen: Agreed. For Dedicated you'd provision GPU pool sized for expected peak but with autoscale/burst and fallback to Hosted if needed. That hybrid model often gives best cost control.
[08:38] Priya Sharma: For the pilot, would we get access to a sandbox Dedicated pool?
[08:42] Lina Rodriguez: Yes, we can provision a small Dedicated sandbox for benchmarking. It'd be a short-term reserved capacity with shared ops; we'll include the cost and trial terms in the workbook.
[08:53] Aisha Khan: Procurement question — do you require minimum annual commitment for Dedicated?
[08:58] Lina Rodriguez: We have monthly and annual commitments. For pilots we can do a month-to-month sandbox with an agreed max spend. Longer commitments get better unit pricing.
[09:07] Priya Sharma: Marcus, can you outline the micro-benchmark you'll run?
[09:11] Marcus Chen: We'll run three profiles: 1) chat latency profile emulating your p95 target with warm KV cache turned on/off, 2) async long-seq throughput for 4k summarization, and 3) mixed traffic to measure resource contention. We'll collect p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, GPU utilization, and cost-per-1k-token estimates.
[09:30] Daniel Ortiz: How much data do you need to run the cache tests?
[09:33] Marcus Chen: We'll need representative prompt variety and a set of repeated templates to seed the cache. If you can provide 1000 prompts and traffic histogram that's ideal.
[09:41] Priya Sharma: We'll prepare that.
[09:44] Aisha Khan: On invoicing — how granular is the billing for Hosted? Is it daily, monthly?
[09:49] Lina Rodriguez: Hosted billing is monthly with usage breakdowns per route/model in the Console; you can also enable daily alerts and spend caps. Dedicated has committed fees plus usage for bursts. All invoicing is line-itemed.
[10:01] Priya Sharma: One more question about model variants: do you let us pin a model variant for a route and automatically fall back if capacity's constrained?
[10:08] Marcus Chen: Yes, Redwood routing policies support pinning and fallback: you can set primary model, fallback model and region routing. The runtime will auto-failover to fallback when capacity is low to keep service available.
[10:19] Daniel Ortiz: What about data residency? We have some EU customers.
[10:22] Lina Rodriguez: We have region routing and customer data residency controls. For strict residency, Private deployments or dedicated regional clusters are recommended.
[10:30] Priya Sharma: Ok, let's talk timeline — we want a pilot to start in mid-November if possible.
[10:34] Lina Rodriguez: That's doable. We'll prioritize the benchmark in next two weeks and share the pricing workbook within 48 hours after this call.
[10:41] Priya Sharma: Excellent.
[10:43] Marcus Chen: Quick callouts: 1) we'll simulate network RTT in our benchmark to reflect your app latency, 2) test cold start and warm cases, and 3) include a quantized model variant to show delta in throughput/cost.
[10:56] Daniel Ortiz: Great. Aisha, anything else from procurement?
[10:59] Aisha Khan: Just please include data handling, SLA and KMS sections in the pilot doc. We'll want the legal touchpoint after we see the numbers.
[11:07] Lina Rodriguez: Will do.
[11:10] Priya Sharma: Should we recap next steps?
[11:12] Lina Rodriguez: Sure — I'll send the pricing workbook and pilot template by 2025-10-16. Marcus will run the micro-benchmark and aim to deliver initial results by 2025-10-20. Priya will share the 1k prompt set and traffic histogram by 2025-10-17. Then we'll reconvene to review results and discuss pilot contract.
[11:29] Daniel Ortiz: Sounds good.
[11:31] Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone.
[11:33] Priya Sharma: Thanks all.
[11:35] Lina Rodriguez: Thanks team — talk soon.

Notes on transcript quality: some words auto-transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" -> "K V cash") and model names occasionally mangled. This transcript preserves filler words and short interruptions.
